name: Windmill Hills
description:
The one with the row of tall, thin hills you fly over. Each hill is a steep face up to a narrow peak with a long landing shoulder behind it: hit the face fast and the peak throws you high over the crest, with time in the air for a flip, down onto the shoulder. The hills grow taller along the route, and every valley climbs gently back up to the field, so the trail stays level and the next hill can be taken at speed.

Route and apples, in order:
1. Start field under a steep bank, then the smallest hill. Apple 1 sits just past its crest: ride over it and you touch it. Teaches that the peaks throw you.
2. Second hill: apple 2 floats above the far side of the crest. Needs speed carried up the face.
3. Third hill, with a beehive and a skylark on its shoulder: apple 3 higher still.
4. Mill hill: the mill turns on the crest, and apple 4 hangs beyond its sails. Full throttle up the face.
5. Flip hill, the tallest, a pine on the peak: apple 5 at the top of the arc. The longest air of the trail, enough for a backflip.
6. Finish: a last, smaller hill with the flower floating high above its crest. Hit it with speed to hop up to it, or roll back down the face for a longer run-up.

Skill: carrying speed into a steep face (momentum). Leaning to keep the front down on a face and to level the bike in the air helps, but the bot finishes without either, so they are not required. Flips are optional: the flip hill gives about 1.9 s of air, and a backflip lands.

After a miss: nothing on the trail ends a run except a bad landing. Every valley is an open bowl. Too slow up a face, roll back and take a longer run-up. Past an apple without it, turn, ride back over the hill and up the previous landing shoulder, turn again and use the shoulder as a run-up: it costs about ten seconds, not the run. Each comeback was measured with the bot from a standstill in the valley beyond.
lesson: Big air. A row of tall, thin hills: carry speed up each steep face and the peak throws you high over the crest onto its landing shoulder, with time in the air to level the bike, or to flip it.
alsoNew: A farmland hillside of tall, narrow hills with a patch of nature on each, skylarks that take off from the peaks, and the mill turning on its own hill.
